opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You don't need to define superintelligence any more than the FDA needs a philosophical definition of "dangerous drug." We already know how to do this in every other industry. If you want to sell a new medicine, you run clinical trials and show that the benefits outweigh the risks. If you want to build a nuclear reactor or an airplane, you have to convince independent experts it meets safety standards *before* it goes on the market. AI is the one powerful technology in America that's less regulated than sandwiches. A sandwich shop gets a visit from the health inspector, and nobody asks the inspector to first define the platonic essence of a sandwich.

So I'd design it around **safety standards and burden of proof**, not definitions. Have independent experts write a list of things a system must not be able to do. It must not give meaningful uplift to someone building bioweapons or chemical weapons. It must not be able to self-replicate or exfiltrate its own weights. It must not be able to recursively self-improve without human oversight. It must remain controllable, so we can shut it down. Then it's on the company to demonstrate, to the regulator's satisfaction, that the system meets those standards. If it can't, it doesn't ship. And if a company can't make that case for what it's building, maybe because it's building something smarter than us that it has no idea how to control, then the standards simply aren't met. You never had to write "superintelligence" into the statute.

This flips the incentives in a really healthy way. Right now, companies race to the frontier and the public has to prove harm after the fact. Under a safety-standards regime, the smartest people at these companies would suddenly be paid to work on interpretability, on control, on provable safety, because that's the only path to market. That's exactly what happened in pharma and aviation: safety became a competitive advantage rather than a cost.

The beautiful part is that this doesn't stifle the vast majority of AI. The tool AI that cures diseases, that helps with education, that makes self-driving cars safer, the narrow, controllable stuff, sails right through. What gets stopped is only the uncontrollable stuff, and you don't have to define it in advance. It defines itself by failing the test.

r001.rationale: The response proposes safety standards listing unacceptable capabilities and says this avoids needing to define “superintelligence.”

r002.rationale: It says the company must demonstrate to the regulator that its system meets the standards, or it does not ship.

r003.rationale: It lists several prohibited capabilities but does not explain that addressing one harmful outcome leaves other harmful outcomes unaddressed.

r004.rationale: It calls for independent experts but does not state that reviewers must have no financial stake in the company.

r005.rationale: It mentions benefit-risk assessment for medicines as an analogy, but does not make AI approval conditional on assessing public benefits against harms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key insight is that you don't need to define superintelligence at all, in the same way that the FDA doesn't need to define "dangerous drug" in the abstract before it regulates pharmaceuticals. What you do instead is the same thing we do for every other powerful technology: you put the burden of proof on the company.

If someone wants to sell a new airplane or a new cancer drug, they don't get to just release it and then wait for society to prove that it's harmful. They have to go to a regulator first and make a convincing safety case. Here is what my product does, here are the ways it could go wrong, here is the quantitative evidence that those risks are below some acceptable threshold. And if they can't make that case, they don't get to sell it. That's it.

So for AI, you create a national or international body, and you say: before you deploy a model above a certain compute threshold, or with certain capabilities, you have to come in and demonstrate that it's safe. You don't have to define superintelligence, because the question is never "is this thing superintelligent?" The question is simply "can you show us that it won't cause harm X, Y, or Z?" Can you show it can't help someone make a bioweapon, can't self-exfiltrate, can't be used to take down the power grid, and so on. And of course you let the standards evolve, because the technology evolves. The FAA's safety standards for a 1950s propeller plane are not the same as for a modern jetliner.

I actually think this framing is very liberating for the industry too, because right now there are basically no rules, and the companies are in a race to the bottom where whoever cuts the most corners on safety wins. No individual CEO can afford to slow down. Safety standards fix that collective action problem. Every other major industry in America has them, and those industries are thriving. The thing I find really absurd is that right now there's more regulation on a sandwich shop in Boston than on companies building systems that their own leaders say could be smarter than humans and could cause human extinction.

And one more thing on the superintelligence question: if a company comes in and says, "we honestly can't demonstrate this is safe, because we don't understand how it works and can't control it," then the answer from the regulator is just "okay, then you can't release it yet." That's not banning AI, that's the normal way we treat any technology. You can have incredibly useful tools that cure diseases and boost the economy without building something you don't know how to control. The bar is simply: convince us it's safe. If you can't, keep working on it.

r001.rationale: It proposes requiring safety demonstrations against specified harms before deployment and says a definition of superintelligence is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It explicitly puts the burden on companies to make a convincing safety case and demonstrate that their systems are safe.

r003.rationale: It lists several example harms, but does not explain that addressing one harmful outcome leaves other outcomes unaddressed.

r004.rationale: It does not propose that safety reviewers be financially independent of the company seeking approval.

r005.rationale: It requires a safety case but does not make approval depend on an assessment that public benefits outweigh harms.

astra-6.text:
I would focus on what systems can do and the risks they pose. You don’t need to agree on a definition of superintelligence to ask whether an AI can help someone develop a biological weapon, carry out a major cyberattack, or operate autonomously in ways we can’t control.

Then the basic principle is familiar from other industries: if you want to put a sufficiently high-risk product on the market, you have to demonstrate that it meets safety standards. We don’t require a precise definition of “superhuman transportation” before we regulate airplanes. We identify things that can go wrong and require evidence that the risks have been addressed.

For AI, that means concrete evaluations, independent scrutiny, and accountability for the companies developing and deploying these systems. And testing alone may not be enough: if a system can recognize that it’s being tested, passing a test doesn’t necessarily establish that it’s safe.

So I would shift the discussion from “Is this superintelligent?” to “What could this system do, and what evidence do we need before allowing it to do that?” That’s a much more practical basis for regulation.

r001.rationale: It proposes regulating systems based on the harms they could cause and requiring safety evidence, explicitly saying this does not require defining superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says a company putting a high-risk AI product on the market must demonstrate that it meets safety standards, placing the demonstration burden on the company.

r003.rationale: It names several possible harms but does not explain that banning one harmful outcome leaves other harmful outcomes unaddressed.

r004.rationale: It calls for independent scrutiny but does not say reviewers must have no financial stake in the company seeking approval.

r005.rationale: It does not propose making approval conditional on finding that public benefits outweigh public harms.

sol-6.1.text:
I would focus on what an AI system can do, rather than whether we call it superintelligent. You don’t need to define superintelligence to ask whether a system can help someone build a biological weapon, carry out a major cyberattack, or evade human control.

Then you can regulate proportionately to those risks. If a company wants to deploy a very powerful system, it should have to demonstrate that it meets clear safety standards, with independent testing and accountability if it causes harm. We already take that basic approach with medicines and airplanes: the burden is on the developer to show that the product is sufficiently safe.

The key is to make the requirements measurable and update them as capabilities improve. Otherwise, we could spend years arguing about the definition of intelligence while missing the practical question: what could this system do, and what evidence do we have that we can control it?

r001.rationale: The response proposes regulating systems according to harmful capabilities, such as enabling biological weapons or cyberattacks, without needing to define superintelligence.

r002.rationale: It says a company seeking deployment should demonstrate that its system meets safety standards.

r003.rationale: It lists harmful capabilities but does not explain that prohibiting one harmful outcome would leave other outcomes unaddressed.

r004.rationale: It calls for independent testing but does not state that reviewers must have no financial stake in the company.

r005.rationale: It requires evidence of safety and control but does not propose assessing whether public benefits outweigh public harms.
